correctness.rationale: An exact positive-equilibrium scalar reduction gives the unique nondegenerate onset. Jacobian rank-one similarity verifies stable and saddle branches. Two strict majorization inequalities follow from explicit Schur--Ostrowski derivative signs; bounds and unattained boundary limits are proved, and both shared second-order expansions are derived analytically. A standalone checker passed 1,400 varied equalization/bound/eigenvalue samples and four curvature families, treated only as diagnostics.

originality.rationale: In the full accessible text of arXiv:2605.01021, the original reduced ODE and scalar saddle-node relation are established, along with special equal-rate formulas and a two-dimensional unequal-rate formula. The inspected result does not claim, establish or compare the global strict majorization order of both K_c and the critical product coherence X_c for all D>=3, nor their sharp simultaneous quadratic heterogeneity corrections. New differential comparison arguments and a sharp fixed-budget extremal theorem have been supplied. Actual indexed and public literature searches found no equivalent statement for this precise model; unindexed or reparameterized prior formulations remain possible.
residual_risks: Some older or reparameterized product-cooperative ODE literature might already give the Schur order without naming the torus-Kuramoto model.
The original scalar equation makes the coupling ordering comparatively short; priority and degree of novelty beyond its premises are not independently certified.
Related hypergraph and sphere articles were not all read completely; their abstracts do not establish full-document noncoverage.

value.rationale: For the first-order onset of the recently introduced product-coupled multidimensional torus-Kuramoto model, the fixed-total-width allocation is an intrinsic robustness question. The theorem supplies an all-dimensional sharp majorization comparison and extrema for two physically interpretable onset observables, including a common variance penalty and a threshold ratio tending to e. This complements, rather than repeats, the original location formula and is not an arbitrary finite enumeration.
